label: SCENE STUDY
title: In the Mood for Love
hook: The affair in this film happens entirely off-screen.

slides.b: Mrs. Chan's husband and Mr. Chow's wife are in the film, but only as the backs of heads and voices from another room. Wong Kar-wai never lets you look at the two people actually having the affair. You are left with the two who got left.

slides.h: They are acting, until they aren't
slides.b: The scenes that look like romance are role-play. They act out how their spouses might have started, then how a confrontation would go. By the time the feeling is real, neither of them can tell which lines were practice.

Yumeji's Theme wasn't written for this film. Shigeru Umebayashi composed it for Seijun Suzuki's Yumeji in 1991. Wong borrowed it and repeats it until it stops sounding like music and starts sounding like the same evening happening again.

slides.q: He remembers those vanished years. As though looking through a dusty window pane, the past is something he could see, but not touch.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Quizás, Quizás, Quizás
pairs.note: Sung in Spanish he learned by ear. It's in the film, and the title is the whole plot: perhaps, perhaps, perhaps.

pairs.label: READ THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Intersection (Tête-bêche)
pairs.note: The Hong Kong novella Wong thanks in the credits.

caption:
every time I rewatch this I notice the same thing: nobody in it ever does anything. they eat noodles. they pass on a staircase. and somehow it's the most charged film I know.

swipe for the three things that make it work.

label: LOOK CLOSER
title: Paris Street; Rainy Day
hook: There is no rain in this painting.

slides.b: Search the air and you won't find a single streak of rain. Caillebotte only painted what rain does: the shine on the cobbles, the grey light, the umbrellas. He lets the street tell you the weather.

Reproductions make it look like a snapshot. In the room the figures are nearly life-size and you feel you could walk into them. The couple on the right are about to, and they aren't looking where they're going.

A green lamp post splits the canvas down the middle, the way a photograph gets cropped by accident. In 1877 this was a brand-new Paris of wide, identical boulevards, and he painted how lonely it is to be well dressed in a city that size.

slides.h: The rich one who paid for the others
slides.b: Caillebotte had family money. He bought Monet's, Renoir's and Degas's paintings when nobody else would, and paid Monet's rent. He left the lot to France. Much of what hangs in the Musée d'Orsay is there because of him.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Gymnopédie No. 1
pairs.note: Written in the same city eleven years later. Same walking pace.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Playtime (1967)
pairs.note: Another Paris of glass and grey, where everybody is slightly lost.

caption:
I stood in front of this for twenty minutes once and a guard asked if I was alright.

it's the umbrellas. they're all the same umbrella. that's the whole modern world, in 1877.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Frances Ha
hook: That run through New York is borrowed from a French film.

slides.b: In 1986 Leos Carax had Denis Lavant sprint and cartwheel down a Paris street to David Bowie's Modern Love in Mauvais Sang. In 2012 Greta Gerwig runs through Manhattan to the same song. His run is a breakdown. Hers is just a good day.

It looks like 1960s stock, but it was shot on a Canon 5D Mark II, a consumer camera, in colour, then turned black and white. Much of the music is Georges Delerue, lifted from French films of the New Wave years.

You don't learn why it's called Frances Ha until the end. She writes her full name, Frances Halladay, for the mailbox of her first flat of her own. The paper is too long for the slot, so she folds it. A life that almost fits.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Modern Love
pairs.note: Obviously. Then watch the Mauvais Sang scene straight after.

pairs.label: READ THIS AFTER
pairs.title: The Dud Avocado
pairs.note: 1958. An American girl being a glorious mess in Paris.

caption:
"I'm not a real person yet" is the most accurate line ever written about being 27.

the run is the famous bit, but the mailbox is the one that gets me.

label: LINER NOTES
title: Pink Moon
hook: 28 minutes. Two nights. One overdub.

slides.b: Nick Drake booked Sound Techniques in London late at night, when the studio was empty. Just him, a guitar and the engineer John Wood. No strings, no band, no producer. He was done in two sessions.
The only thing added afterwards is the piano line on the title track, which he played himself. Everything else is one voice and one guitar, in tunings people are still arguing about.

It barely sold. He died in 1974, aged 26. In 1999 Volkswagen put the title track in a Cabrio commercial, and the album reportedly sold more in the following weeks than it had in the quarter century before.

slides.q:
Now we rise
And we are everywhere
slides.by: From the Morning. Also carved on his headstone.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS NEXT
pairs.title: I Remember
pairs.note: His mother's home recordings from the 1950s. You will hear where he got it.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: A Skin Too Few (2000)
pairs.note: A 48-minute documentary, mostly filmed in his bedroom.

caption: the whole record is shorter than an episode of television and I've still never managed to do anything else while it's on.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: The Fall
hook: Four years, twenty-odd countries, and one director's own money.

slides.b: Tarsem made commercials and music videos, and for years he tacked shoots for this film onto those jobs, paying for much of it himself. The stepwell at Chand Baori, the blue walls of Jodhpur, the red dunes of Namibia: those are places, not effects.

Catinca Untaru was six, Romanian, and barely spoke English. To keep her reactions real, Lee Pace stayed in a wheelchair on set and most of the crew were told he was paralysed. When she misreads a note in the film, that's a real mistake they kept.

slides.h: A story told by a liar
slides.b: A broken stuntman invents an epic to trick a child into stealing morphine for him. So the fantasy keeps bending: she pictures an 'Indian' as a man from India, because that's what she knows. It is a film about who a story belongs to.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Symphony No. 7, II. Allegretto
pairs.note: It runs under the black-and-white opening. Best title sequence of its decade.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Yo Ho Ho (1981)
pairs.note: The small Bulgarian film this is based on. Almost nobody has seen it.

caption:
for years you basically couldn't watch this legally anywhere and people passed it around like contraband. now there's a restoration. no excuses.

the most beautiful film I know and it isn't close.

label: SHELF NOTES
title: The Hour of the Star
author: Clarice Lispector
hook: A novel with thirteen titles.

slides.b: The Blame Is Mine, or The Hour of the Star, or Let Her Deal With It, or The Right to Scream, or Singing the Blues, or Cheap Tearjerker, or Discreet Exit Through the Back Door. Lispector printed them all and refused to choose.

A typist from Brazil's poor northeast who is bad at typing, lives on hot dogs and Coca-Cola, and listens to a radio station that only tells the time. She doesn't know she is unhappy. The book is under a hundred pages.

The story is told by a man called Rodrigo S.M., who is ashamed to be writing about someone poor from a comfortable desk and puts off starting for pages. Lispector makes the guilt of telling the story part of the story. She died weeks after it came out.

slides.q: Who has not asked himself at some time or other: am I a monster or is this what it means to be a person?

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Preciso Me Encontrar
pairs.note: Rio, 1976. A samba about needing to go and find yourself.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: A Hora da Estrela (1985)
pairs.note: The film version, made by a director who started film school at 37.

caption:
you can read this in one sitting and then you'll think about it for roughly the rest of your life.

start here if you've never read Lispector.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Paris, Texas
hook: The lead doesn't speak for nearly half an hour.

slides.h: A man walks out of the desert
slides.b: Travis appears in a red cap and a dusty suit, collapses, and says nothing. His brother drives him across two states trying to get a word out of him. When one finally comes, it is the name of a town: Paris.

He finds his wife working in a Houston peep-show booth where she can't see the customer. He turns his chair so he can't see her either, and tells their story as if it happened to strangers. The story goes that Sam Shepard dictated the speech down a phone line mid-shoot.

Ry Cooder built the score on Blind Willie Johnson's Dark Was the Night, Cold Was the Ground: no words, just humming and a slide. In 1977 NASA put that same recording on the Voyager Golden Record and sent it out of the solar system.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Dark Was the Night, Cold Was the Ground
pairs.note: Three minutes. Lights off.

pairs.label: READ THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Motel Chronicles
pairs.note: The book Wenders wanted to film before the two of them wrote this instead.

caption:
Harry Dean Stanton spent thirty years as "that guy" in other people's films. this was his first lead. he was in his late fifties.

the booth scene is on slide 3. I'm not over it.

label: LOOK CLOSER
title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa
hook: The subject of this picture is not the wave.

slides.b: It comes from a series called Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji. Fuji is the small triangle in the middle, easy to mistake for another crest. The wave is just what happens to be in front of it.

slides.h: Thirty men are about to die
slides.b: Three long boats are under that claw, with rowers bent flat against the hulls. They were fast boats that carried fresh fish to market. Japanese is read right to left, so to its first viewers the wave was coming straight at them.
That blue is Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment from Europe that had only recently become cheap in Japan. It is part of why the print looked so new. A copy cost about as much as a bowl of noodles.

slides.q: Nothing I did before the age of seventy was worthy of attention.
slides.by: Hokusai, who made this at about seventy

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: La Mer
pairs.note: He put this very wave on the cover of the score in 1905.

pairs.label: READ THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Hokusai: A Life in Drawing
pairs.note: He changed his name some thirty times and moved house over ninety.

caption:
he was about seventy, broke, and had been struck by lightning once. then he made the most reproduced image in the history of art.

it's on your friend's tote bag. look at it properly anyway.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Aftersun
hook: The dance floor she can never quite get across.

slides.b: Last night of the holiday. Calum pulls eleven-year-old Sophie up to dance and she is mortified. The film cuts to adult Sophie in a strobe-lit rave, reaching for him, while the song is stripped back to Bowie and Mercury's bare voices. A lyric turns into a fact.
A lot of what we see is MiniDV footage that Sophie is rewatching as an adult. The film is honest about what a holiday video is: a few minutes of proof for a week you mostly can't rebuild.

Nobody says what's wrong with Calum. You get a cast on his wrist he can't explain, a tai chi book, a rug he can't afford, and his back shaking on a hotel bed. Charlotte Wells trusts you with the rest.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Tender
pairs.note: It plays in the film slowed down and warped, like a tape left in the sun.

pairs.label: READ THIS AFTER
pairs.title: The Years
pairs.note: Another attempt to rebuild a past from photographs.

caption:
I watched this on a tuesday afternoon and then called my dad.

it's a film about one holiday and also about the fact that you only understand your parents when you reach the age they were.

label: LINER NOTES
title: World of Echo
hook: A cello, a voice, and a lot of echo.

slides.b: Arthur Russell was a cellist from Iowa who ended up in downtown New York writing disco twelve-inches and minimalist pieces in the same years. World of Echo is neither. It is him alone, murmuring over an amplified cello through delay.
He was famous for never finishing anything. He would take rough mixes out on the Staten Island Ferry and listen on headphones, back and forth across the harbour, then go home and change them again.
He died in 1992, aged 40, almost unknown outside a few clubs and lofts. He left behind around a thousand tapes. Most of what people now love by him was released after he was gone.

slides.q: I'm watching out of my ear.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS NEXT
pairs.title: That's Us / Wild Combination
pairs.note: His pop side. The happiest sad song there is.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Wild Combination (2008)
pairs.note: The documentary. His parents in Iowa will break your heart.

caption: put this on with headphones on public transport, which is how he listened to it. it won't make sense for ten minutes and then it will be the only thing that does.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Paterson
hook: A bus driver called Paterson, in Paterson, writes poems. That's it.

slides.b: He wakes without an alarm, drives the 23 bus, eats lunch by the waterfall, walks the dog, has one beer. Seven days. The only disaster in the whole film is caused by the dog, and it is devastating.

The poems Paterson writes are by Ron Padgett, of the New York School, some written for the film. The one the little girl reads him was written by Jarmusch. Adam Driver, for his part, went and got a real bus licence.

Every other film about an artist is about being discovered. This one says the work can live in a notebook in a basement and still be the centre of a life. It is the least anxious film ever made about making things.

slides.q:
We have plenty of matches in our house.
We keep them on hand always.

pairs.label: READ THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Paterson
pairs.note: The long poem about the same New Jersey town, by a doctor who wrote between patients.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: The Paterson score
pairs.note: Jarmusch's own band. Slow guitars that sound like a bus idling.

caption:
the bulldog won an award at Cannes. she'd died a few months earlier. I think about that more than is reasonable.

watch this on a sunday when you feel behind in life.

label: SHELF NOTES
title: The Book of Disquiet
author: Fernando Pessoa
hook: This book was found in a trunk.

slides.b: Pessoa died in Lisbon in 1935 having published very little. He left a wooden trunk holding more than 25,000 sheets: poems, horoscopes and fragments written under dozens of invented authors, each with a biography and a style of his own.

Among them were hundreds of undated scraps for a diary by one Bernardo Soares, an assistant bookkeeper who looks out of an office window in downtown Lisbon and thinks. No plot. No order. It was first published 47 years after Pessoa died.

Because he left no sequence, every edition is an editor's guess. Two translations can be noticeably different books. The upside: it was never finished, so you can open it anywhere and you are not reading it wrong.

slides.q: My past is everything I failed to be.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Estranha Forma de Vida
pairs.note: Fado. “Strange way of life.” He would have recognised it.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Lisbon Story (1994)
pairs.note: A sound man wanders the same streets with a microphone and a Pessoa paperback.

caption: not a book you finish. a book you keep next to the bed and open at random when you can't sleep, which is how he wrote it.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Columbus
hook: A love story about buildings.

slides.b: Columbus, Indiana has about 50,000 people and buildings by Eero Saarinen, I.M. Pei and Richard Meier. From the 1950s a local engine company offered to pay the architect's fee for public buildings, so a small Midwestern town filled up with modernism.

Jin asks Casey to stop reciting tour-guide facts about a building she loves and say what actually moves her. She answers. Kogonada puts the camera behind glass and drops the sound. We watch her explain it and never hear a word.
Kogonada made video essays on Ozu and Bresson before this, and it shows: still frames, doorways, people placed off-centre. The pseudonym is a nod to Kogo Noda, Ozu's screenwriter.

slides.q: It's asymmetrical, but also still balanced.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: The Columbus score
pairs.note: Nashville ambient duo. It sounds the way a glass wall looks at dusk.

pairs.label: READ THIS AFTER
pairs.title: The Architecture of Happiness
pairs.note: On why a building can make you feel understood.

caption: nobody talks about this film and I don't know why. it's two people walking around a town in Indiana looking at a bank. it wrecked me.

label: LOOK CLOSER
title: The Bedroom
hook: These walls were never meant to be blue.

slides.b: Van Gogh described the walls in a letter as pale violet. The red in his purple paint has broken down over a century, leaving the blue behind. The room you know is not quite the room he painted.

The first, from 1888, was damaged by damp while he was in hospital. A year later, in the asylum at Saint-Rémy, he painted it again from memory, and then a small one for his mother and sister. The versions hang in Amsterdam, Chicago and Paris.

It's the only room he ever really had to himself, in the Yellow House in Arles. The walls look crooked because the room actually was. He wanted a painting that did the work of sleep, and he made it during the least restful year of his life.

slides.q: Looking at the painting should rest the mind, or rather, the imagination.
slides.by: Vincent to his brother Theo, October 1888

pairs.label: READ THIS AFTER
pairs.title: The Letters of Vincent van Gogh
pairs.note: He was as good a writer as he was a painter. Start in Arles, 1888.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Spiegel im Spiegel
pairs.note: Ten minutes of the stillness he was trying to paint.

caption:
two chairs, two pillows, two of everything, for a man who lived alone and was waiting for a friend to come and stay.

once you see that, it's a different painting.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Past Lives
hook: The ending is two people waiting for a taxi.

slides.b: Nora walks Hae Sung to his car. They stand facing each other on an East Village pavement and the film just holds. Nothing is said. Then she walks back to her husband on the stoop and cries, for the first time in the film.

slides.h: Who are they to each other?
slides.b: It starts with strangers in a bar looking at three people across the room, an Asian woman between an Asian man and a white man, and guessing. The whole film is the answer, and by the end you know the guessers were all wrong.
Celine Song reportedly kept Teo Yoo and John Magaro from meeting until they shot the scene where their characters meet. The stiff hello in that doorway is two actors actually sizing each other up.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Quiet Eyes
pairs.note: Written for the end credits. The score is by two members of Grizzly Bear.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Comrades: Almost a Love Story (1996)
pairs.note: Two migrants who keep just missing each other for ten years.

caption: the thing I love is that there's no villain. the husband is kind. the old flame is kind. it's just that one life is all you get.

label: LINER NOTES
title: Either/Or
hook: The quietest man at the 1998 Oscars.

slides.h: A white suit and one guitar
slides.b: March 1998. On the same bill as Celine Dion, a songwriter from the Portland bar circuit walks out alone in a white suit and plays Miss Misery. Gus Van Sant had put his songs in Good Will Hunting. He lost to My Heart Will Go On.

Either/Or came out a year earlier on a tiny label. Much of it was recorded in houses around Portland rather than studios. The sound is his trademark: the vocal sung twice and layered, so a whisper carries like a choir.

After eleven songs about bars, bad nights and people leaving, the album ends with Say Yes: two minutes, major key, a morning after where somebody stays. He once said it was the only optimistic song he had.

slides.q:
I'm in love with the world
through the eyes of a girl
who's still around the morning after

pairs.label: PLAY THIS NEXT
pairs.title: Between the Bars
pairs.note: Same album. A love song written from the point of view of the drink.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Heaven Adores You (2014)
pairs.note: The documentary, with a lot of unreleased music in it.

caption:
he later said the Oscars were like walking around on the moon for a day. fun, and he wouldn't want to live there.

Say Yes is on slide 4.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Still Walking
hook: One family lunch. Fifteen years of things nobody says.

slides.b: A family gathers at the parents' house on the anniversary of the eldest son's death. They cook, bicker about a car, take a photo. Kore-eda wrote it after losing his own mother, and you can tell: every detail of the kitchen is exact.

Each year the mother invites the young man her son drowned rescuing. He sits there sweating and apologising. Afterwards she says, quite calmly, that she'll keep inviting him. She wants him to feel it once a year. It is the coldest line in a warm film.
She puts on an old pop single, Blue Light Yokohama, and hums along. The title is a line from its chorus. Then you learn why she kept that record, and the tune is never innocent again.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Blue Light Yokohama
pairs.note: 1968. A sweet, swaying hit single with a knife in it.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: When a Woman Ascends the Stairs (1960)
pairs.note: People compare Kore-eda to Ozu. He says he's closer to Naruse. He's right.

caption:
the corn tempura scene made me hungry and then homesick, in that order.

Kiki Kirin as the mother is one of the great performances. funny, petty, grieving, all in the same sentence.

label: SHELF NOTES
title: The Summer Book
author: Tove Jansson
hook: The Moomin author wrote one perfect book for adults.

slides.h: An island, a child, a grandmother
slides.b: Six-year-old Sophia and her grandmother spend a summer on a tiny island in the Gulf of Finland. Twenty-two short chapters. They argue about God, build a miniature Venice in the marsh, and break into a neighbour's house. Nothing else happens.

Early on you are told, in passing, that Sophia's mother has died. It is not mentioned again. Jansson wrote the book soon after losing her own mother, and the whole thing is about a grief that nobody in it will say out loud.

She knew the life. Jansson spent close to thirty summers on Klovharun, a bare skerry in the Pellinge archipelago, in a one-room cabin with no electricity. Sophia is based on her niece, who now looks after the Moomins.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Höstvisa
pairs.by: Erna Tauro, words by Tove Jansson
pairs.note: “Autumn Song”, 1965. She wrote lyrics too.

pairs.label: READ THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Fair Play
pairs.note: Two women artists who share a life and an attic. Even quieter.

caption:
there's a chapter where the grandmother is too tired to play and the kid is furious about it, and it's the truest thing I've read about being old and being six.

read it in july if you can. read it in january if you can't.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Punch-Drunk Love
hook: The pudding scheme was real.

slides.b: Barry buys pallets of pudding because the air miles on the label are worth more than the pudding. That happened. In 1999 a Californian engineer called David Phillips spent about $3,000 on pudding cups and collected 1.25 million frequent-flyer miles.
He Needs Me is sung by Shelley Duvall as Olive Oyl in Robert Altman's Popeye (1980). Harry Nilsson wrote it. Anderson dropped it into the middle of this film and Jon Brion built the score around it.

slides.h: One blue suit, the whole film
slides.b: Barry never changes out of it. Lena is always in red or pink. Between scenes the screen dissolves into washes of colour made by the artist Jeremy Blake. It is an Adam Sandler comedy that takes the anger in every Adam Sandler comedy seriously.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: He Needs Me
pairs.note: Wobbly, off-key, and the most romantic thing on the soundtrack.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS NEXT
pairs.title: Here We Go
pairs.note: The end-credits song. A waltz that sounds like it's falling down stairs.

caption: "I have a love in my life. it makes me stronger than anything you can imagine." shouted down a phone at a mattress salesman. cinema.

label: LOOK CLOSER
title: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte

image.aic: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte

hook: Stand close enough and this painting disappears.

slides.b: Seurat was twenty-five. He made dozens of sketches on the island, then spent two years in the studio building a ten-foot canvas out of small touches of pure colour, on the theory that the eye would mix them better than a palette could.
He used a new yellow that began to darken within his lifetime. The sunlit grass has gone ochre and brown in places. He never knew how much. He died at thirty-one.
Forty-odd people on a day off and not one conversation. Everyone faces sideways like figures on an Egyptian wall. Only the little girl in white, dead centre, looks straight out at you.

In Ferris Bueller's Day Off, Cameron stares at that child while the camera cuts closer and closer until her face is only dots. John Hughes said the more he looks, the less he sees, and that it's what Cameron fears about himself.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Sunday
pairs.note: From Sunday in the Park with George, the musical about this canvas. The last chord is the painting.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Ferris Bueller's Day Off (1986)
pairs.note: For the museum scene alone. Two minutes, no dialogue.

caption:
a teen comedy from 1986 contains the best piece of art criticism I know and it has no words in it.

find the monkey. bottom right.
wiki: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Portrait of a Lady on Fire
hook: A film with almost no music, on purpose.

slides.b: What you hear is footsteps, fire, charcoal on canvas and the sea. Sciamma wanted music to be as rare for the audience as it was for a woman on a Breton island in 1770, who might hear an orchestra a handful of times in her life.

slides.h: Then the women start to sing
slides.b: An hour in, a group of women around a fire begin clapping and chanting in Latin: fugere non possum, I cannot flee. It was written for the film by Para One and Arthur Simonini. After an hour of silence it lands like a storm.

Years later Marianne sees Héloïse across a concert hall as the orchestra plays the storm from Vivaldi's Summer, a piece she once picked out badly on a harpsichord for her. The camera stays on Héloïse's face for the whole movement.

slides.q: He doesn't make the lover's choice, but the poet's.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: The Four Seasons: Summer, III. Presto
pairs.note: You will never hear it as background music again.

pairs.label: READ THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Metamorphoses, Book X
pairs.note: Orpheus and Eurydice, the story they argue about by candlelight.

caption:
page 28.

if you know, you know. if you don't, watch it tonight and come back.

label: LINER NOTES
title: songs
hook: Recorded in a room that sounded like the inside of a guitar.

slides.b: Big Thief's tour was cancelled and a relationship had just ended. Adrianne Lenker rented a one-room cabin in the mountains of western Massachusetts. She said the pine room made her feel as if she was inside an acoustic guitar, and asked an engineer friend to drive up.

It was recorded to analogue tape with no computer in the room. You can hear the rain on the roof, birds, wind chimes and the chair. Two albums came out of it together: songs, and a second called instrumentals.

The best-known track is a list of small shared memories: a mango, a dog bite, a Christmas with somebody's family. Then a chorus that just wants to stop talking about it. Break-up songs are usually speeches. This one is a photo album.

slides.q:
I don't wanna talk about anything
I wanna kiss, kiss your eyes again

pairs.label: PLAY THIS NEXT
pairs.title: zombie girl
pairs.note: Same record. Listen for the birds coming in on the second verse.

pairs.label: READ THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Devotions
pairs.note: Another person who went into the woods and paid close attention.

caption: you can hear the room on this record. that's the whole appeal. it sounds like someone playing to nobody at 6am because they couldn't sleep.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: The Lunchbox
hook: A love story where the two leads never share a frame.

slides.b: Mumbai's dabbawalas carry around two hundred thousand home-cooked lunches to offices every day, sorted by painted codes, and are famous for almost never getting one wrong. The film is about the one that goes to the wrong desk.

A neglected wife and a widower weeks from retirement start writing notes in the tiffin. Irrfan Khan and Nimrat Kaur filmed their halves apart. You watch two people fall for each other entirely through what they cook and what they leave uneaten.

Ila's best friend is a neighbour she shouts to through the kitchen window, who sends down spices in a basket on a rope. You never see her. Batra first set out to make a documentary about the dabbawalas, and it shows in how real the city sounds.

slides.q: Sometimes the wrong train will get you to the right station.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Mera Dil Bhi Kitna Pagal Hai
pairs.note: From Saajan (1991). The film hums it, and then you can't stop.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Photograph (2019)
pairs.note: Same director, same city, even quieter.

caption:
Irrfan Khan eating lunch alone and slowly realising someone cooked it with care is better acting than most people's whole careers.

the ending is left open and I've decided what happens. don't tell me otherwise.

label: SHELF NOTES
title: Letters to a Young Poet
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
hook: The most famous advice in literature came from a 27-year-old.

slides.b: Franz Xaver Kappus was nineteen and miserable at a military academy that Rilke had also attended and also hated. He posted his poems to the poet and asked if they were any good.

He declines to judge them. Instead he asks whether Kappus would die if he were forbidden to write. Ten letters follow over five years, from Paris, Italy and Sweden. Rilke was broke and had not yet written the books he is known for.
Kappus published the letters in 1929, three years after Rilke died, and left his own out. He became an army officer and a writer of popular novels. The young poet did not, in the end, become a poet.

slides.q: Be patient toward all that is unsolved in your heart and try to love the questions themselves.
slides.by: Letter four, tr. M.D. Herter Norton

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Flight from the City
pairs.note: Seven notes on a piano, over and over, getting kinder.

pairs.label: READ THIS AFTER
pairs.title: The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge
pairs.note: His only novel. What he was actually writing in Paris between the letters.

caption: it helps to know he was 27, skint and unsure of himself when he wrote these. it's not wisdom from a mountain. it's one anxious person being gentle to another.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Chungking Express
hook: This was made as a holiday from another film.

slides.b: In 1994 Wong Kar-wai was stuck in the edit of his desert epic Ashes of Time. To clear his head he made this, fast, on the streets of Hong Kong, often writing a scene the day it was shot.

The apartment that Faye sneaks into and quietly rearranges belonged to the cinematographer, Christopher Doyle. It sat right beside the Central to Mid-Levels escalator, which is why she can spy on it from the moving walkway.
California Dreamin' plays so often it becomes furniture. Then over the ending you hear Dreams by The Cranberries, sung in Cantonese by Faye Wong, who was already a pop star when she took the part.

slides.q: If my memory of her has an expiration date, let it be ten thousand years.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: 夢中人 (Dream Lover)
pairs.note: The Cranberries cover. Arguably better than the original. I said it.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Fallen Angels (1995)
pairs.note: It began life as this film's third story, then got too big.

caption:
a man buys thirty cans of pineapple that expire on his birthday because his girlfriend left him on april fools' day. that's the first ten minutes.

no film has ever made being lonely look this much fun.

label: LOOK CLOSER
title: The Child's Bath
hook: This is an American painting that learned everything from Japan.

slides.b: The floor tilts up, the jug sits at the bottom edge, and you see the two figures from above as if standing over them. In 1890 Cassatt went to a huge show of Japanese woodblock prints in Paris. She went back again and again, and her pictures changed.

Look at how flat it is. The striped dress, the papered wall, the carpet: each is a block of pattern laid next to another, the way a printmaker would. The only soft, round thing in the picture is the child.
Everything points to the basin. Her hand holds the small foot, the child's hand presses on her knee. Nobody is posing. Both of them are looking at the water. It is a painting about paying attention.

slides.h: The only American in the room
slides.b: Cassatt came from Pennsylvania, settled in Paris, and was invited by Degas to show with the Impressionists, the only American who did. She later talked wealthy friends back home into buying their work, which is partly why so much of it is in American museums.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Clair de Lune
pairs.note: Paris, the same years, the same love of things seen through water.

pairs.label: LOOK AT THIS NEXT
pairs.title: Woman Bathing (1890–91)
pairs.note: One of the colour prints she made straight after that exhibition. Degas was jealous of the line.

caption: people file Cassatt under "mothers and babies" and walk past. look at the geometry instead. this is as radical as anything the men were doing.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Before Sunrise
hook: The best scene is two people not looking at each other.

slides.b: A Vienna record shop. Céline and Jesse squeeze into a listening booth and put on a folk record. For about a minute, in a single shot, each looks at the other only when the other looks away. That's all. That's the scene.

The song is Come Here by Kath Bloom, a Connecticut folk singer whose 1980s records with the guitarist Loren Connors were pressed in tiny numbers. She had mostly stopped releasing music. This scene is why people went looking for her.

Linklater based the film on a night in 1989 spent walking around with a woman he met in a toy shop, Amy Lehrhaupt. They lost touch. She died in 1994, before the film came out, and he did not find out until years later. Before Midnight is dedicated to her.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Come Here
pairs.note: Try to listen to it with someone and hold eye contact. You can't.

pairs.label: READ WHAT THEY READ
pairs.title: Georges Bataille & Klaus Kinski
pairs.by: On the train, before they speak
pairs.note: She has Bataille. He has Kinski's memoir. Make of that what you will.

caption: everyone talks about the talking in these films. the listening booth has no dialogue at all and it's the bit I'd save from a fire.

label: LINER NOTES
title: Just Another Diamond Day
hook: She wrote this album from the back of a horse-drawn wagon.

slides.h: London to the Hebrides, on foot
slides.b: In 1968 Vashti Bunyan gave up on being a pop singer and set off for Scotland with a horse called Bess, a dog and a wagon, heading for a commune Donovan had promised. It took the better part of two years. The songs are what she sang on the road.

Joe Boyd produced it. Robert Kirby, who wrote Nick Drake's string parts, did the arrangements, and members of Fairport Convention played. It came out in 1970 and vanished. She was so stung she stopped making music.

She raised children and kept animals. In the late nineties she typed her own name into a search engine and found the album was selling for hundreds of pounds and a new generation of folk musicians were calling it a masterpiece. Her second album came out in 2005.

slides.q:
Just another diamond day
Just a blade of grass
Just another bale of hay
And the horses pass

pairs.label: PLAY THIS NEXT
pairs.title: Train Song
pairs.note: A 1966 single that also sank. It's perfect.

pairs.label: THEN THIS
pairs.title: Lookaftering
pairs.note: The follow-up, thirty-five years late. Her voice hadn't aged a day.

caption:
thirty-five years between first and second album. she just assumed it was bad and got on with her life.

think about that next time something you made gets no likes.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Toni Erdmann
hook: The funniest scene of the decade is a woman singing Whitney Houston against her will.

slides.b: Ines is a management consultant in Bucharest with no time for anything. Her father turns up uninvited in a bad wig and false teeth, introduces himself to her clients as a life coach called Toni Erdmann, and will not leave.

At a stranger's family party he sits at a keyboard and announces that his daughter will sing. She has no way out. Sandra Hüller does Greatest Love of All in full, furious, flat-out, and somewhere in the second verse it stops being a joke.

slides.h: Two hours forty, and a comedy
slides.b: Maren Ade lets scenes run long past the point other directors would cut, so embarrassment has time to turn into something else. There is a hug near the end, involving a very large Bulgarian costume, that I'd put against any in cinema.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Greatest Love of All
pairs.note: You will never hear it the same way. Sorry.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Everyone Else (2009)
pairs.note: Her film before this. A couple on holiday, slowly finding out who they are.

caption:
it's nearly three hours of a dad embarrassing his daughter and at the end I cried in a way I wasn't prepared for.

call your dad. or don't, it's complicated, the film knows that too.

label: SHELF NOTES
title: Having a Coke with You
author: Frank O'Hara
hook: The best love poem of the century is about a soft drink.

slides.h: He wrote on his lunch break
slides.b: Frank O'Hara started at the Museum of Modern Art selling postcards at the front desk and ended up a curator. He wrote poems fast, at lunch, on shop typewriters, and stuffed them in drawers. Friends had to dig them out to publish them.

He wrote it in 1960 for Vincent Warren. It lists great art, the Polish Rider at the Frick, the Impressionists, Marino Marini, and waves all of it away. He would rather look at one person drinking a Coke under a tree.
That's the thing. It isn't someone who doesn't care about paintings. It's a man who spent his working life among masterpieces telling you, with total authority, that they lose.

slides.q: I look at you and I would rather look at you than all the portraits in the world

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: For Frank O'Hara
pairs.note: Written by a friend in 1973, seven years after O'Hara died. Barely there, on purpose.

pairs.label: READ THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Lunch Poems
pairs.note: Small enough for a coat pocket, which is the point.

caption:
there's film of him reading this in 1966, cigarette in hand, a few months before he died. find it.

if someone sends you this poem, marry them.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Perfect Days
hook: This film began as a commission about public toilets.

slides.b: Shibuya had seventeen public toilets redesigned by architects including Tadao Ando, Shigeru Ban and Kengo Kuma. Wim Wenders was invited to shoot something short about them. He came back with a feature, filmed in a little over two weeks.

slides.h: A man with good taste and no phone
slides.b: Hirayama's cassettes: The Animals, Patti Smith, Lou Reed, Otis Redding, Nina Simone. His paperbacks, from the cheap shelf: Faulkner's The Wild Palms, Aya Koda's Trees, Patricia Highsmith's Eleven. The film never explains how a toilet cleaner came by all this.

Every lunchtime he photographs the same tree on a film camera. The Japanese word for sunlight filtering through leaves is komorebi, and the film closes on its definition: it exists only once, at that moment.

Nina Simone's Feeling Good plays in the van and the camera stays on Koji Yakusho for the whole thing, laughing and crying in the same breath. He won Best Actor at Cannes more or less for those two minutes.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Aoi Sakana
pairs.note: Japanese folk from 1972, off one of his tapes. The deep cut of the soundtrack.

pairs.label: READ THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Eleven
pairs.note: The short stories his niece borrows. Start with The Terrapin.

caption:
"next time is next time. now is now."

I've started noticing tree shadows on walls because of this film and I'm not even annoyed about it.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Drive My Car
hook: The opening credits arrive forty minutes in.

slides.b: By the time the titles appear you have watched a marriage, a betrayal and a death. Then the cast names roll over a red car on a motorway, two years later, and the actual story starts. It runs three hours and does not waste one.

In Haruki Murakami's short story the Saab 900 is a yellow convertible. Hamaguchi made it a red hardtop. A closed roof let him record long conversations cleanly, and the red shows up against every grey road in Hiroshima.

Hamaguchi has actors read the script aloud, with no emotion at all, over and over, until the words are in the body. Feeling is saved for the take. The film shows the method itself, in rehearsals for an Uncle Vanya played in several languages, one of them Korean Sign Language.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Drive My Car (Kafuku)
pairs.note: The main theme. Made for motorways at night.

pairs.label: READ THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Uncle Vanya
pairs.note: Sonya's last speech is the ending of the film, signed instead of spoken.

caption:
three hours, mostly people talking in a car, and I'd have happily taken four.

the sign-language ending is the best final scene of the decade and I will not be taking questions.

label: LINER NOTES
title: Colour Green
hook: Recorded in the early seventies. Released in 2006. She never meant you to hear it.

slides.b: Between about 1970 and 1973 a young German actress recorded fourteen songs at home, in English, on a tape machine. Then she decided against a career, raised a family, and the tapes went in a box for thirty years.
Her son burned the songs to CD as a family present. A copy reached J Mascis of Dinosaur Jr., who passed it to a small label. It came out in 2006 and people could not believe it was real.
You can hear that she isn't singing to anyone. There's no audience in her head. She appears for a few moments in Wim Wenders' Alice in the Cities, and that is close to her entire public career.

slides.q:
Tonight when I came home from work
there he, unforeseen, sat in my kitchen

pairs.label: PLAY THIS FIRST
pairs.title: I Lost Something in the Hills
pairs.note: Two and a half minutes. You'll know by the first line.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Alice in the Cities (1974)
pairs.note: Look for her on the ferry.

caption:
the best album of 2006 was thirty-three years old.

play it when it's raining and you're doing the dishes. that's what it was made during.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Petite Maman
hook: A girl meets her mother at eight years old. Both of them are eight.

slides.b: Nelly's grandmother has died. While her parents clear the house, she walks into the woods and finds a girl her own age building a hut, with her mother's name and her mother's face. The film never says how. It doesn't need to.

The two girls are played by twins, Joséphine and Gabrielle Sanz, who had never acted before. Sciamma shot it in the autumn of 2020, in a few weeks, mostly in one house and one wood. It runs seventy-two minutes.
As in Portrait of a Lady on Fire, there is no score until a single moment: the girls paddle a boat towards a strange pyramid and a synth song bursts in. It is called Music of the Future.

slides.q: You didn't invent my sadness.
slides.by: Marion, aged eight, to her future daughter

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: La Musique du Futur
pairs.note: The only music in the film. Children's choir, big synths, total joy.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: My Neighbor Totoro (1988)
pairs.note: Same woods, same absent mother, same refusal to explain the magic.

caption:
seventy-two minutes. shorter than most football matches. it says more about mothers and daughters than films twice as long.

the pancake scene is the hardest two children have ever laughed on camera.

label: SHELF NOTES
title: Stoner
author: John Williams
hook: The first paragraph tells you he dies forgotten. Then you read 280 pages anyway.

slides.b: Page one tells you William Stoner taught at a Missouri university for forty years, never rose above assistant professor, and that few people remembered him after he died. That is the plot. Williams dares you to care, and you do.

slides.h: A farm boy hears a sonnet
slides.b: He is sent to college to study agriculture. In a compulsory literature class a teacher reads a Shakespeare sonnet and asks him what it means. He can't answer. He changes his whole life because of that silence.

It sold about two thousand copies in 1965 and went out of print. It was reissued in 2006, and a few years later a French translation made it a bestseller across Europe. Williams had been dead for nearly twenty years.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Peace Piece
pairs.note: One left-hand figure, repeated for six minutes, and a whole life on top of it.

pairs.label: READ THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Butcher's Crossing
pairs.note: His western. Completely different, just as merciless.

caption:
nothing happens to this man. a bad marriage, a job, one love affair, some books. it's the most gripping novel I've read in years and I can't fully explain why.

the last three pages. my god.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Cléo from 5 to 7
hook: Ninety minutes of waiting, told in ninety minutes.

slides.b: A pop singer is waiting for the result of a biopsy. The film follows her across Paris in close to real time, with chapter cards giving the minutes. Despite the title, it stops half an hour early.
It opens in colour on a tarot reading: only the cards and the hands. The moment the camera looks up at the women's faces, it switches to black and white and stays there.

Halfway through, Cléo pulls off her wig, puts on a plain black dress and walks out. Until then she has been looked at, in every mirror in Paris. From here she does the looking. Her pianist, by the way, is played by Michel Legrand, who wrote the score.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Sans toi
pairs.note: The song she rehearses in her flat. Legrand's music, Varda's words.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: The Beaches of Agnès (2008)
pairs.note: Her own life story, told at eighty, walking backwards on a beach.

caption: there's a silent short hidden in the middle of this starring Jean-Luc Godard and Anna Karina, and he takes his dark glasses off for it. Varda got him to do that. nobody else could.

label: SCENE STUDY
title: Yi Yi
hook: A boy who photographs the backs of people's heads.

slides.b: Eight-year-old Yang-Yang is given a camera and uses it to take pictures of the backs of heads. When his uncle asks why, he says: you can't see it yourself, so I'm helping you. That is the film explaining itself.

slides.h: A wedding, a birth, a funeral
slides.b: Three hours with one Taipei family, starting at a wedding and ending at a funeral. The grandmother is in a coma and the doctor tells them to talk to her. One by one they find out how little they have to say.
Edward Yang won Best Director at Cannes for it in 2000. He never made another feature and died in 2007. For years it had no proper cinema release in Taiwan, the place it is about.

slides.q: I want to tell people things they don't know. Show them stuff they haven't seen.

pairs.label: WATCH THIS AFTER
pairs.title: A Brighter Summer Day (1991)
pairs.note: Four hours. Clear a Sunday. Worth every minute.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Moonlight Sonata, I. Adagio
pairs.note: Something patient, played by somebody who isn't showing off.

caption:
it's three hours long and when it ended I wanted to know what happened to every single one of them.

if you only ever watch one Taiwanese film, this one.

label: LINER NOTES
title: Music for Nine Post Cards
hook: This album was written for a building.

slides.b: Hiroshi Yoshimura wrote these nine pieces at home on a keyboard and a Fender Rhodes, thinking about clouds, shade and a tree outside a window. He took the tape to a new art museum in Tokyo, and they played it in the galleries.

In Japan it was called kankyō ongaku: sound designed to sit in a room like light does. Yoshimura went on to write music for train stations and show homes. He said he wanted pieces you could ignore, that would still change the air.

He died in 2003, known to very few. Around 2017 his records were reissued and uploads began surfacing in millions of people's recommendations. A man who made music for empty rooms became the sound of everybody's desk.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS FIRST
pairs.title: Blink
pairs.note: Track two. A handful of notes that somehow slow your pulse.

pairs.label: THEN THIS
pairs.title: Through the Looking Glass
pairs.note: 1983. Same scene, more marimba, recorded in two days.

caption:
I put this on to work and forgot it was playing, which he would have taken as the highest compliment.

windows open, if you can.

label: SHELF NOTES
title: The Pillow Book
author: Sei Shōnagon
hook: A thousand years ago a woman at the Japanese court invented the list post.

slides.b: Sei Shōnagon served Empress Teishi in Kyoto around the year 1000. The story goes that the Empress was given a bundle of good paper and Shōnagon said she'd make a pillow of it, meaning a bedside notebook. She filled it with whatever crossed her mind.

Much of it is lists. Things that make the heart beat faster. Things that have lost their power. Hateful things, which include a guest who talks too long and a lover who fusses over his hat while leaving. She is funny, vain, and extremely precise.

At the same court, Murasaki Shikibu was writing The Tale of Genji. In her diary she called Shōnagon dreadfully conceited. Two of the great books of world literature were written by women who worked down the corridor from each other and did not get on.

slides.q: Things that make one's heart beat faster: sparrows feeding their young. To pass a place where babies are playing.

pairs.label: PLAY THIS WITH IT
pairs.title: Asleep Among Endives
pairs.note: A voice and a guitar, a thousand years later, with the same attention to small things.

pairs.label: READ THIS AFTER
pairs.title: Essays in Idleness
pairs.note: A monk's version, three centuries on. Grumpier.

caption:
she would have been incredible at this app.

"a lover who fusses over his hat while leaving" has been living in my head for years.
